title: 87 ft of cracked clay sewer lateral lined in Allied Gardens
summary: A homeowner who had been snaking his line every six to eight months finally got a permanent fix: TSR hydro-jetted a root ball 23 feet out and lined the full 85-foot clay lateral in a single day.
body:
The situation

This Allied Gardens homeowner had been paying to have his sewer cleared every six to eight months for a couple of years, and each time the interval got shorter. He had put off a real repair because every quote involved digging up the yard and replacing the pipe.

TSR ran a camera down the line first. The repeated cable cleanings had been chewing at the old clay pipe, and the video showed cracking along much of its length. About 23 feet from the house sat a large root ball that was the real cause of the backups: with the pipe that restricted, anything more than light use pushed sewage back into the home.

The fix

The line measured roughly 85 feet to the city connection. Rather than open the yard, TSR hydro-jetted the roots and scale out of the clay pipe, then inverted a resin-saturated liner through the full run and cured it in place. The homeowner had a neighbor over to watch.

The whole repair was done in under a day, and the bathrooms were back in use that evening. He had expected two or three days of work and a five-figure excavation bill; the lining came in at a fraction of that and left the yard untouched.

title: 62 ft cast iron sewer lined under a front-yard playground in Anaheim Hills
summary: A family with an elaborate built-in playground in the front yard could not excavate. TSR lined the 60-foot cast iron sewer beneath it without moving a single piece of equipment.
body:
The situation

The homeowners had spent years nursing a failing sewer along, and by the time they called TSR the line needed more than another cleaning. The complication: a large, permanently installed playground filled the front yard directly over the sewer's path. Digging was off the table.

A camera inspection confirmed the cast iron lateral was deteriorating along its full length but had not collapsed anywhere, which made it a good candidate for cured-in-place lining.

The fix

TSR cleaned and lined about 60 feet of cast iron from the house to the street through a single access point. Nothing above ground was disturbed. The homeowner mentioned afterward that when they put the playground in they had never thought to check the sewer first; the liner meant they did not have to choose between the two.

title: 119 ft residential sewer lined after root damage in Arcadia
summary: After 30-plus trouble-free years, a serious backup revealed root-cracked pipe along a long Arcadia lateral. TSR lined all 119 feet in one day.
body:
The situation

Arcadia lots tend to be large, which means long sewer laterals and a long stretch of pipe the homeowner is responsible for. This owner had lived in his house since the early 1980s without a single sewer problem until a major backup sent him looking for help.

TSR's camera inspection found the cause: tree roots had worked into the pipe and, over time, cracked it open where they entered. The line ran roughly 120 feet before reaching the city main.

The fix

Excavating a run that long, and restoring the landscaping afterward, would have been expensive and slow. TSR cleaned the pipe and installed a continuous cured-in-place liner over the full 119 feet. The job took one day, and the homeowner has a seamless pipe that roots cannot re-enter.

title: 137 ft of mixed cast iron, clay and ABS replaced by pipe bursting in Beverly Hills
summary: A property owner had a lining quote for 135 feet of patchwork sewer. TSR's camera found three different pipe materials and recommended bursting in a brand-new HDPE line instead, done in one day.
body:
The situation

The owner, a financial analyst, had already been quoted for lining about 135 feet of sewer and wanted a second opinion. TSR ran a free camera inspection and found a line assembled from three eras of repair: sections of cast iron, clay and ABS, with roots at the transitions.

Why bursting instead of lining

TSR performs both lining and pipe bursting and recommends whichever suits the pipe. Lining a run made of three different materials is possible, but bursting replaces it outright: a bursting head is pulled through the old pipe, breaking it apart while towing a new, fused HDPE pipe into its place. It needs only two small access pits, which are restored when the work is done.

The result

All 137 feet were replaced in a single day with a continuous, jointless HDPE pipe. The owner told the crew he has several other properties in Beverly Hills and intends to have TSR rehabilitate all of them.

title: Condo HOA: 140 ft pipe burst plus 86 ft CIPP liner under mature landscaping in Burbank
summary: A 20-unit Burbank condominium had backups on two separate 6-inch clay lines under mature landscaping. TSR burst one run and lined the other, reinstating all ten unit connections, with no trenching.
body:
The situation

The HOA president for a 20-home condominium community in Burbank called TSR after half the units began experiencing sewer backups. The problem lines ran beneath mature landscaping the board did not want disturbed, and several members had asked whether a trenchless approach was possible.

Line one: 140 ft of 6-inch clay, pipe burst

The first line was a 6-inch vitrified clay collector serving ten units. After the camera survey, TSR recommended pipe bursting: a bursting head was pulled through the old clay, fracturing it while drawing in a new fused HDPE pipe. Roughly 140 feet were replaced this way, and each of the ten unit connections was reinstated afterward.

Line two: 86 ft of 6-inch clay, CIPP lined

The second run carried flow from the property to the city sewer and was choked with roots. TSR hydro-jetted the roots out, then installed a resin-impregnated liner, inflated it with a bladder and let it cure in place, leaving a seamless new pipe inside the old one.

The result

Two rehabilitated sewer lines, no excavation through the landscaping, and a saving the board put at well over $25,000 against a conventional dig-and-replace. This is the kind of multi-connection, mixed-method job that a lot of trenchless outfits will not take on.

title: 55 ft cast iron sewer replaced by pipe bursting under trees in Canoga Park
summary: A homeowner cleaning up after a basement backup wanted the sewer fixed without losing the trees over it. TSR burst in a new line the same day.
body:
The situation

The call came from a Canoga Park homeowner who had just finished cleaning up a sewage backup in his basement. He knew the pipe ran under mature trees and had no interest in cutting them down to reach it.

TSR's camera inspection found a large crack in the cast iron lateral. Because the pipe's alignment was sound, it was a straightforward candidate for pipe bursting.

The fix

Work started immediately. The crew burst out all 55 feet of cast iron and pulled in new HDPE, working from two small pits well clear of the root zones. The trees stayed, the basement stayed dry, and the homeowner said he would be sending his neighbors TSR's way.

title: 45 ft sewer lined behind an ornamental retaining wall in Chula Vista
summary: The sewer ran under a retaining wall the owner described as a work of art. TSR lined the failing 45-foot lateral without touching it.
body:
The situation

Chula Vista has plenty of older housing with original cast iron and terra cotta laterals, and this one was at the end of its life: the camera showed a pipe that was cracked, separating and shedding material. The catch was a large, elaborate retaining wall built directly over the line. Digging it out was not something the owners were willing to consider.

The fix

Cured-in-place lining needs only an access point, not a trench, so the wall was never in play. TSR cleaned the 45-foot run, installed and cured a new liner, and left the homeowners with a seamless pipe and an intact wall. Every remaining foot of old pipe out to the city connection was covered by the liner, so there is no weak section left to fail later.

title: 86 ft of root-filled clay sewer replaced by pipe bursting beneath garden statuary in Encino
summary: A second-opinion call: 86 feet of 4-inch clay under a lawn full of marble statues and water features. TSR burst in a new line the same day at roughly half the competing quote.
body:
The situation

The homeowner already had one trenchless quote and wanted another. His front lawn was set with marble statuary and water features he had collected from around the world, and the 86-foot clay sewer ran directly under them. Roots had found the joints and the line was backing up.

The fix

TSR's inspection confirmed the pipe was a good candidate for bursting. Because TSR owns its bursting and lining equipment rather than renting it, the price came in at about half the other bid. The crew arrived with everything needed to do the job on the spot, burst the full 86 feet of clay and pulled in new HDPE, and finished the same day. Not one statue moved.

title: 44 ft cast iron sewer lined to save a family tree in Fountain Valley
summary: The tree in the front yard had been planted by the owner's grandfather the year she was born. Its roots were in the sewer. TSR jetted and lined the 44-foot cast iron line without harming it.
body:
The situation

Roots had invaded the cast iron lateral and the homeowner's first concern was not the pipe but the tree above it, planted by her grandfather on the day she was born. She wanted to know whether the line could be lined rather than dug.

The fix

TSR's camera showed heavy root intrusion and damage to the pipe wall. The crew hydro-jetted the roots out at high pressure, re-inspected to confirm the host pipe could hold a liner, then installed and cured a resin liner over the full 44 feet. The work took about a day. The sewer now runs like new and the tree is still standing.

title: 96 ft hillside sewer replaced by pipe bursting in Glendale
summary: Hillside lots, heavy tree cover and old terra cotta: a familiar Glendale combination. TSR replaced 96 feet of root-damaged pipe with fused HDPE by pipe bursting.
body:
The situation

Glendale's hillside neighborhoods are green, which is exactly the problem for old clay and cast iron sewers: roots follow the moisture into every joint. This homeowner was getting the seasonal backups that come with it, worst in spring when root growth picks up.

The TSR technician had just completed a job on the same street and recognized the pattern before the camera confirmed it: root intrusion and cracking through the terra cotta run.

The fix

For a long, root-damaged run like this, TSR recommended pipe bursting over lining. A bursting head fractured the old clay while pulling a new 96-foot HDPE pipe into place. HDPE is jointless and the ends are heat-fused, so there is nowhere for roots to get back in. Two small access pits were restored when the work was done.

title: 64 ft cast iron sewer cleaned and lined in Granada Hills
summary: A homeowner asked for an evaluation before committing. The camera showed a root-filled cast iron line that was still sound enough to line, and TSR lined all 64 feet.
body:
The situation

The owners knew the sewer was not working properly but not why. They asked TSR to inspect and tell them whether their line could be lined at all, since they had no intention of excavating the property.

The fix

The camera showed cast iron with roots throughout, but no collapse, which is the key requirement for cured-in-place lining. TSR hydro-jetted the line clean, installed a liner over the 64-foot run and cured it in place. The pipe now has a smooth, continuous interior and the homeowners avoided any digging.

title: 73 ft clay sewer with roots at every joint lined in Hillcrest, San Diego
summary: Roots had found every ten-foot joint in this Hillcrest clay lateral. TSR jetted it clean and installed a 73-foot liner in a day.
body:
The situation

Older Hillcrest homes sit on original clay sewer laterals laid in ten-foot sections, and every joint is an entry point for roots. This line had cracks as well as a root mass at essentially every joint.

The fix

TSR cleared the roots with a hydro-jetter, which also scours the pipe interior so the liner bonds properly. With modern resins the condition of the host pipe matters less than people expect; it only needs to hold the liner in shape for the few hours it takes to cure. The crew lined the full 73 feet and the homeowner got a pipe that is, in practical terms, better than the original, without a trench through the yard.

title: 75 ft cast iron sewer lined same-day after a downstairs backup in La Jolla
summary: Fifteen years of mature landscaping, one root-cracked cast iron lateral. TSR inspected and lined the 75-foot line the same day, with no digging.
body:
The situation

The homeowner had planted and shaped her garden herself over fifteen years and had never had a sewer problem until a backup flooded the downstairs bathroom. The camera found what mature landscaping usually means for cast iron: roots in the pipe and cracks where they entered.

The fix

TSR's trucks carry enough material to line a typical residential run on the spot, so the crew went straight from inspection to repair. They cleaned and lined the full 75 feet that afternoon. The post-lining video showed a pipe that looked new, and the garden was exactly as she had left it.

title: 55 ft cast iron sewer lined under a deck and decades of landscaping in La Jolla
summary: A 1960s La Jolla home with the sewer running under the front deck and trees the owner had planted over several decades. TSR lined the 55-foot cast iron line without disturbing either.
body:
The situation

The owner had been putting off the repair for a long time. Her home dated from the 1960s, the backups were confined to the downstairs bathroom guests used, and the cast iron lateral ran out under the front deck and through landscaping she had been planting for decades. She did not know exactly where the line ran, only that she did not want it dug up.

The fix

TSR's camera survey located the pipe and found severe root buildup as the cause of the backups. The run to the street was only about 55 feet. The crew lined it in a fraction of the time an excavation would have taken, and she stayed in the house while they worked. The bathroom has not backed up since.

title: 38 ft of 50-year-old clay sewer lined in La Mesa
summary: Twice-a-year backups from cracked, root-invaded clay pipe. TSR lined the 40-foot lateral in a day.
body:
The situation

The homeowner's clay sewer was more than fifty years old and had been backing up once or twice a year. She told the technician she never wanted to clean up another one. The camera showed root-cracked terra cotta over the roughly 40-foot run to the city main.

The fix

TSR cleaned the line and installed a cured-in-place liner over the full length, finishing in a day. A seamless liner has no joints for roots to exploit, which is what ends the annual backup cycle rather than postponing it.

title: 22 ft sewer lined to close a home sale in La Mesa
summary: A pre-purchase camera inspection found cracked, root-filled clay pipe. TSR jetted and lined the 22-foot section, delivered a post-lining video, and the sale went through.
body:
The situation

The buyers had asked for a sewer inspection before closing, which was sensible: it showed a cracked clay pipe full of roots. The sale contract required the seller to fix it, and the listing agent needed a repair that was fast, would not tear up a nicely landscaped yard, and would satisfy the buyers.

The fix

TSR came out promptly, cleared the roots with a hydro-jetter, lined the 22-foot section and handed over a post-lining inspection video showing the new liner in place. The new owners got a sewer covered by TSR's lining warranty, the yard was untouched, and the sale closed.

title: 80 ft cast iron and clay sewer lined beneath two remodeled bathrooms in Laguna Beach
summary: Years of garage flooding every time the back toilet flushed, and an excavation quote far over budget. TSR mapped two connections and lined 80 feet of mixed pipe out to the alley from one small access point.
body:
The situation

Every flush of the rear bathroom sent water into parts of the garage, and the family had been living with periodic rooter visits for years. An excavation quote came in well over budget, which is when they went looking for a trenchless contractor.

TSR's camera survey showed a 4-inch cast iron drain leaving the back of the house and running about 80 feet to the alley, changing to clay for the last ten feet. Two connections had been added when the home was put on a raised foundation years earlier, and two remodeled outdoor bathrooms sat directly over the damaged section. Roots throughout, as is typical in Laguna.

The fix

The crew hydro-jetted the roots out, mapped the branch connections, and lined the run through a single small access pit, reinstating the connections afterward. The result is one continuous pipe from the house to the alley that roots cannot get back into, with both bathrooms and the rest of the property untouched.

title: 69 ft cast iron sewer lined same-day after repeated jetting in Brentwood, Los Angeles
summary: Two hydro-jettings in six months and a backup anyway. TSR found root-cracked cast iron and lined the 69-foot line the day of the inspection.
body:
The situation

The homeowner in the Brentwood area had paid to have her line hydro-jetted twice in six months, and the third backup came up through the downstairs bathroom. Jetting clears roots; it does not repair the cracks they leave behind, and the camera showed the cast iron pipe had cracked where the roots came in.

The fix

The technician had enough liner on the truck to start immediately. He jetted the line one more time to prepare the pipe, inverted the liner through the full 69 feet and let it cure for about five hours. She now has a seamless pipe with no joints for roots to find, and no more twice-yearly jetting bills.

title: 82 ft cast iron sewer replaced by pipe bursting in Los Angeles
summary: The owner had a lining quote for about 80 feet. TSR's inspection measured 82 feet of deteriorating cast iron and offered pipe bursting for a new HDPE line at a lower cost.
body:
The situation

Pipe bursting has become the preferred trenchless method for a lot of Los Angeles laterals because it delivers a brand-new pipe rather than a liner inside the old one, and usually for less. This owner had a lining quote in hand when he called TSR for a second look.

The fix

The camera measured the line at exactly 82 feet: cast iron, breaking down, with roots that needed clearing. TSR burst the old pipe and pulled in new HDPE from two small pits, finishing in a day. The owner got a fully replaced, jointless sewer at a meaningful saving over the lining bid.

title: 55 ft broken cast iron sewer replaced by pipe bursting before a baby arrived in Oxnard
summary: A new homeowner with a pregnant wife and two inches of sewage on the bathroom floor. TSR found a broken joint halfway to the street and replaced the whole 55-foot line by bursting.
body:
The situation

The owner had bought the house about fourteen months earlier without a sewer inspection and had been paying for cleanings ever since. The last backup put two inches of raw sewage across the back bathroom, and with his wife expecting their first child he wanted it fixed for good.

TSR's free camera inspection found a cast iron pipe with a large crack and a broken joint roughly halfway to the street, with soil washing into the line.

The fix

A break that lets dirt in is not a candidate for a spot repair. TSR burst the full 55 feet and pulled in a new HDPE pipe, giving him a sewer with no joints and no weak spots before the baby arrived. Oxnard has a great deal of aging cast iron, and TSR owns its bursting equipment outright, which is why other contractors in the area often subcontract this work to them.

title: 65 ft of rotted cast iron sewer lined without touching the patio in Pacific Beach
summary: Pitted cast iron was snagging paper and building blockages. TSR lined the entire 65-foot run from below ground, leaving yard and front patio untouched.
body:
The situation

Pacific Beach has a lot of original cast iron in the ground, and as it ages the interior pits and flakes. Paper catches on the rough surface, dries between flushes, and builds up until the pipe blocks. The camera inspection showed the pipe wall was compromised along its full length, not just at one spot.

The fix

TSR recommended lining the entire lateral rather than chasing individual bad sections. The crew installed a continuous liner over about 65 feet of rotted cast iron in one day. Everything happened underground: no trench in the yard, and the front patio was never touched. The post-lining video shows a smooth, seamless interior where the pitted iron used to be.

title: 57 ft sewer lateral jetted and relined after a basement backup in Pacific Beach
summary: A technician working a block away responded the same day to a backed-up basement and sewer odor, hydro-jetted the line, and returned to reline the 57-foot lateral.
body:
The situation

The homeowner noticed a persistent sewer smell from the downstairs bathroom sink. A TSR technician happened to be on a job a block away and came over the same day. The source was a backup in the basement, complete with drain flies and an odor that had become hard to live with.

The fix

The immediate problem was handled that day with a hydro-jetting to clear the line and get the household functioning. A camera inspection then showed the lateral itself needed rehabilitation, so TSR scheduled the follow-up and relined approximately 57 feet of pipe, again without excavating the property. The odor, the flies and the backups all went with the old pipe.

title: 390 ft of 8-inch clay sewer main CIPP lined with 38 laterals robotically reinstated in Riverside
summary: A homebuilder's due diligence on a Riverside development found separations at every joint of a 390-foot, 8-inch Mission Clay main. TSR lined it and reinstated all 38 lateral tie-ins with a robotic cutter, in about five days.
body:
The situation

A homebuilding company was purchasing a partially built residential community in Riverside and wanted the sewer infrastructure verified before closing. The on-site manager asked TSR to inspect roughly 400 feet of 8-inch main.

The camera survey showed Mission Clay pipe, common in the area, with a small separation at every ten-foot joint. Individually minor; collectively, exactly what a buyer does not want to inherit. The measured length came to 390 feet.

The fix

TSR installed a cured-in-place liner through the full 390 feet of 8-inch main, sealing every joint. The line had 38 lateral connections, and rather than excavating each one to reconnect it, TSR used a robotic cutter inside the lined pipe to reopen every tie-in from within.

The result

The entire rehabilitation took about five days with no trenching along the street. This is the kind of larger-diameter, multi-connection work TSR handles alongside residential laterals, and the builder has since engaged the crew for further projects.

title: 53 ft cast iron sewer lined without disturbing citrus trees in San Diego
summary: Roots at every joint and a deteriorating interior, under a front yard full of lemon and lime trees. TSR lined over 50 feet of cast iron and did not harm a single plant.
body:
The situation

The couple had invested heavily in mature landscaping, including several lemon and lime trees in the front yard, and made clear from the first call that digging was not acceptable. TSR's free inspection of the 4-inch cast iron line found roots at every connection and an interior that was beginning to break down.

The fix

TSR scheduled around the owners and lined just over 50 feet of cracked cast iron from a single access point. Her comment afterward was that not one tree or plant had been touched. She has since put the new line on an annual hydro-jet maintenance schedule to keep it clean.

title: 68 ft terra cotta sewer lined under a driveway for a multi-property owner in San Diego
summary: An investor with six San Diego homes wanted the right trenchless method for a clay line under his driveway. TSR lined it, then relined all his other properties over the following month.
body:
The situation

The owner had done his homework and wanted a trenchless repair; he just was not sure whether bursting or lining was the right call. This was one of six homes he owned in San Diego, and the sewer ran under the front yard and out beneath the driveway.

The camera showed old terra cotta, the orange clay pipe that fills with roots and eventually backs up into the house. With the pipe intact but root-prone, TSR recommended lining.

The fix

TSR lined just over 65 feet of terra cotta, leaving the driveway in place. The post-lining video convinced him: a seamless interior with nothing for roots to grip. He asked whether lining made sense as preventive maintenance, and over the next four weeks had every one of his other San Diego properties relined as well.

title: 60 ft root-cracked terra cotta sewer replaced by pipe bursting in Santa Monica
summary: Frequent backups in a tree-lined Santa Monica neighborhood with small children at home. TSR burst out 60 feet of cracked clay and pulled in new HDPE in a day.
body:
The situation

A busy mother with young children was dealing with increasingly frequent backups. Her street is heavily treed, and the camera showed why: terra cotta pipe full of roots, with cracks throughout where the roots were stressing the joints.

The fix

With that much cracking, TSR recommended replacing the line by pipe bursting rather than lining it. The run was only about 60 feet and the work took a day. Several neighbors came over to watch the new pipe go in, and a few asked about having their own lines done.

title: 49 ft clay sewer lined from inside the house with zero digging in a Santee vineyard
summary: The owner had planted grapevines across the entire property. TSR accessed the cracked clay line from inside the home and lined all 49 feet without disturbing a single vine.
body:
The situation

This homeowner had planted grapevines over most of his property and called TSR on a neighbor's referral to find out whether his sewer could be repaired without digging any of them up. The camera showed old clay pipe with cracks and root intrusion over a roughly 50-foot run.

The fix

The technician was able to access the line from inside the house, so there was no excavation at all, not even an access pit. He had the material on the truck, started around 10 in the morning, and had the full 49 feet lined and cured, with the truck packed, by seven that evening. The vineyard was untouched.

title: 86 ft sewer on the verge of collapse lined in Sherman Oaks
summary: Six-monthly jetting had stopped working and the line was backing up the day after cleaning. TSR's camera showed pipe close to collapse, still just lineable, and lined all 86 feet.
body:
The situation

The homeowner had been managing raw sewage backups by having the line hydro-jetted or rodded every six months. When it began backing up the day after a cleaning, she called TSR. The camera inspection found a pipe in very weak condition and close to collapsing, but not yet collapsed, which was the difference between lining it and digging it up.

The fix

TSR moved quickly and lined the full 86 feet before the pipe could deteriorate further. A cured-in-place liner does not depend on the host pipe for strength once cured, so the weakened original is no longer a concern. She has since referred her brother in Encino for the same repair.

title: 64 ft of root-broken terra cotta sewer replaced by pipe bursting in Studio City
summary: Backups under heavy use, normal use and whenever it rained. TSR burst out about 65 feet of broken clay and pulled in a new line without opening the front lawn.
body:
The situation

Studio City sits on a lot of original cast iron and vitrified clay, and after a wet winter the root growth in those pipes shows up as spring backups. This homeowner's terra cotta line was backing up under heavy use, normal use and every time it rained. She did not want her front lawn dug up.

The fix

The camera showed roots had broken the clay apart in places, which ruled out lining and made bursting the right method. TSR burst the roughly 65-foot run and pulled in new HDPE. When the crew left, she said she could not tell they had been on the property.

title: 79 ft partially collapsed clay sewer replaced by pipe bursting in Thousand Oaks
summary: A heavy fountain delivery had crushed a section of terra cotta sewer. A partial collapse cannot be lined, so TSR burst in a new 79-foot HDPE line.
body:
The situation

The owner described sudden backups at a home in an upscale part of Thousand Oaks. From the description TSR suspected a partial collapse, which the camera confirmed in the terra cotta line. The owner was not surprised: a very heavy fountain had recently been delivered to the front of the property, and the trucks had crossed the sewer's path.

Why bursting

A liner needs a continuous host pipe to follow; a collapsed section stops it. Pipe bursting does not care, because the bursting head breaks the old pipe apart as it pulls the new one through. TSR replaced all 79 feet with fused HDPE from two small pits, restored the pits, and the owner got a new sewer at a fair price without any trench across the property.

title: 60 ft scaled and fractured cast iron sewer replaced by pipe bursting in Westlake Village
summary: Backups a few weeks before a retirement party. TSR found flaking, hairline-fractured cast iron and burst in a new line in time for the guests.
body:
The situation

The homeowner had backups starting and her husband's retirement party a few weeks out. When she gave her address, the TSR technician recognized the street; he had recently burst a failing cast iron line a few doors down. Westlake Village has a great deal of cast iron of the same age.

The camera, run through her cleanout, showed heavy scale, an interior that was flaking, and hairline fractures along the pipe.

The fix

TSR burst out the old cast iron and pulled in about 60 feet of new HDPE. She called after the party to say the plumbing had behaved perfectly with a house full of guests.

title: Shared 66 ft cast iron and clay sewer replaced by pipe bursting for two neighbors in Woodland Hills
summary: Two homes on one lateral, one of them getting most of the backups. TSR found a root ball blocking 75% of the tie-in and burst a new line from the damaged connection to the city main.
body:
The situation

Shared sewer laterals are uncommon but they happen, and they need careful handling: both owners have to agree on the work and on who pays. TSR documented everything up front, then ran the camera. Both homes did share one cast iron line to the street, and a large root ball at the point where the second home tied in was blocking about three-quarters of that connection. The final ten feet before the city main was old clay.

The fix

TSR burst the line from the damaged tie-in all the way to the city sewer, taking out the clay section as well, roughly 66 feet in total, and pulled in new HDPE. The neighbors split the cost and the job was complete in under two days. Both households now share a jointless pipe with no tie-in weak spot.

title: 36 ft cast iron sewer lined to the city main for a home builder in Arvada
summary: A builder who had used lining before sent his own camera video, approved a small spot repair at the cracked section, and had the remaining 36 feet lined to the city sewer the next day.
body:
The situation

The customer was a home builder who had seen trenchless lining work before and knew exactly what he wanted: the warranty, the one-day turnaround, and no trench across the lot. The only difficulty was scheduling; he was rarely on site long enough for a camera inspection.

He solved that by sending over a sewer video he already had. It showed a cast iron line with one badly cracked section and sound pipe beyond it, a good candidate for lining. The job was scheduled for the following day.

The fix

With the owner's approval, the crew opened one small access pit at the damaged spot, repaired the break, and used that opening to shoot a resin-saturated liner through the remaining 36 feet of cast iron to the city connection. A bladder inflated the liner tight against the host pipe while it cured for a few hours, then came out, leaving a continuous new pipe inside the old one. The repair went exactly as the builder expected, which for a customer like that is the point.

title: Abandoned excavation rescued: 75 ft cast iron sewer replaced by pipe bursting in Boulder
summary: Another company dug the wrong spot, left a mess and walked off, leaving the family without a sewer for three days. All Sewer burst in a new 75-foot line and had it working by evening.
body:
The situation

The homeowner called for a second opinion after a bad experience: a previous contractor had excavated a hole in the yard, piled the spoil straight onto the lawn, dug in the wrong place, and then abandoned the job. The family had been without a working sewer for three days.

The technician ran a camera to see what he was actually dealing with. The lateral was about 75 feet of failing cast iron, and the alignment was good enough to burst the entire run rather than patch it.

The fix

Because the trucks carry a full stock of HDPE and bursting gear, work started the same day. The crew set two small access pits, laid the spoil on plywood to protect the lawn, pulled a bursting head through the old cast iron and towed in a new fused HDPE pipe behind it. The sewer was back in service by the end of the day, the pits were closed and the yard restored so that the earlier mess was the only trace anyone had been digging.

title: 47 ft flaking cast iron sewer lined from inside the house, no digging, in Centennial
summary: A homeowner weighing bursting against lining got a camera inspection first. The cast iron was flaking and cracking but intact, so the crew lined all 47 feet from inside the home.
body:
The situation

This Centennial homeowner had done his reading and wanted to know which trenchless method fit his pipe. The camera settled it: the cast iron lateral was shedding its interior and developing small cracks along its length, the early stage of a failure that ends in collapse, but there was no collapse yet.

The fix

Intact pipe means lining is an option, and here it could be done with no excavation at all. The technician shot the liner from a cleanout inside the house all the way to the city main, roughly 47 feet, and let it cure for several hours. A closing camera pass showed a smooth, jointless new pipe where the flaking iron had been.

title: 55 ft of root-cracked cast iron sewer replaced trenchlessly at a 70-year-old Denver home
summary: A kitchen leak in a 70-year-old house led to a camera inspection showing root intrusion and cracking through the cast iron sewer. All Sewer replaced the 55-foot line without opening the yard.
body:
The situation

The homeowners had bought an older Denver house knowing the plumbing would need attention eventually. A leak under the kitchen sink turned out to be the least of it: the drain line and the sewer beyond it were original cast iron, and the camera showed heavy root intrusion and cracking along the run to the street.

The fix

Cast iron of that age corrodes from the inside and there is no repairing it in place, but replacing it no longer means a trench. All Sewer rehabilitated the full 55 feet of 4-inch line trenchlessly, with no disruption to the house or the yard, and the owners got the new sewer they had budgeted for without the excavation they had feared.

title: 78 ft of root-filled terra cotta sewer lined in Denver from a customer-supplied inspection
summary: The homeowner already had a sewer video showing terra cotta failing at every joint. All Sewer reviewed it, confirmed the line could be fully rehabilitated by lining, and did the job without any digging.
body:
The situation

Every lining job starts with a camera inspection, and in this case the customer had already had one done. The footage showed about 78 feet of terra cotta with buildup along the walls and roots entering at every joint, failing in several places, but still continuous.

The fix

The technician reviewed the inspection remotely, confirmed the pipe was a lining candidate, and scheduled the work. The crew cleaned the line and installed a cured-in-place liner over the full 78 feet, sealing every joint the roots had been using. No excavation, and a homeowner who said they would be sending friends and family.

title: University swimming pool: 200 ft of 12-inch drain line CIPP lined on the Denver campus
summary: A leaking pool drain system at a Denver university, lined without fully draining the pool: 200 feet of 12-inch liner weighing roughly 800 pounds wet, installed in a day and leak-tested clean.
body:
The situation

The university's campus pool had a leaking drain system, and the obvious approach, draining the pool and excavating the deck, would have taken the facility out of use for a long stretch. All Sewer proposed lining the drain lines from the surge tank with the pool only half drained, and worked the plan through with school officials before starting.

The fix

Pool piping is among the harder trenchless jobs: long runs, tight bends and a lot of prep. The crew inspected every line first, on the principle that if one section has failed the rest is not far behind, then shot a single 12-inch liner 200 feet from inside the tank through the pool's drain lines. Saturated with resin, the liner weighed close to 800 pounds going in. Every joint and 90-degree turn was sealed.

The result

The installation itself took a day; the inspection and approvals took longer. The post-lining camera survey and a water leak test both passed. What the administration had expected to be a major, disruptive repair became a short closure with a superior result, and the university has since brought All Sewer back for other campus pipelines.

title: 44 ft of near-collapse cast iron sewer lined instead of tearing out the porch and driveway in Lafayette
summary: The standing quote was to tear out the front porch and driveway. All Sewer's camera found cast iron close to collapse but still lineable, and lined the 44-foot run the next day.
body:
The situation

The downstairs guest bathroom had been backing up so often the family had stopped using it. The only quote they had was for a conventional excavation that meant removing the front porch and part of the driveway, a figure the owner simply was not prepared to spend on a house he had bought eight years earlier.

The fix

The inspection showed a severely deteriorated cast iron line, in the technician's judgment close to collapse, but with enough structure left to hold a liner. That made timing important, and the repair was scheduled for the next morning. The crew installed the resin-saturated liner over the full 44 feet, inflated the bladder to press it against the failing iron, and let it cure into a new pipe. A closing camera pass confirmed a clean, working line, at a fraction of the excavation price and with the porch and driveway untouched.

title: Same-day rescue: 67 ft of 1950s cast iron with the bottom rotted out, lined in Lakewood
summary: Four rooter visits in a year and a 1950s cast iron pipe with no bottom left. The technician lined all 67 feet the day of the inspection rather than risk a collapse.
body:
The situation

The homeowner had been having her line cleared for two years, four times in the last twelve months alone. The house dated from the 1950s and so did the cast iron sewer. When the technician ran the camera he found the invert of the pipe, the bottom third, rotted completely away along much of the run: sewage was flowing on soil.

The fix

A pipe in that state can collapse at any time, and once it does, lining is no longer possible. The technician showed the owner the video and turned the appointment into a same-day repair, cleaning what was left of the pipe and installing a liner over the full 67 feet. The homeowner, who had expected days of disruption, was close to tears when it was finished that afternoon.

title: 72 ft of cracked clay sewer lined from inside the house under a yard full of cars in Littleton
summary: The front yard was full of the owner's collection of old automobiles, so digging was out of the question. All Sewer jetted the clay line clean and lined 72 feet from inside the home.
body:
The situation

The owner, an older gentleman, opened the call by saying he would sooner sell the house than pay for an expensive sewer repair. The house was backing up, and the front yard was covered in vintage vehicles he had no intention of moving, which ruled out any kind of excavation on top of the cost.

The fix

The camera showed the expected cracks and root intrusion in the old clay line. The technician hydro-jetted the interior clean, then installed a liner over the 72-foot run from an access point inside the house, so nothing in the yard had to move. The owner kept his cars, kept his house, and got a sewer that would stop backing up, for far less than the number he had been dreading.

title: 48 ft cast iron sewer replaced by pipe bursting between mature shade trees in Thornton
summary: A second-opinion call on a cast iron lateral. Bursting came in as the more economical method and kept the large trees in the middle of the yard untouched.
body:
The situation

The homeowners already had one quote and wanted another. The sewer was cast iron, about 48 feet to the main, and ran past large trees in the middle of the yard that provided the summer shade; keeping them was a condition of the job.

The fix

After walking the property, the technician confirmed bursting would work and would come in below lining for this run. Two small access pits, well clear of the root zones, were all that was needed: the crew pulled a bursting head through the old cast iron and drew in a new fused HDPE pipe with no joints or seams for roots to find. The repair took less than a day, with the owner watching over the crew's shoulder the whole time.

title: 76 ft of root-cracked sewer lined in San Juan Capistrano for $9,800
summary: Another plumber quoted $18,000 to dig up and replace 76 feet of sewer. After researching CIPP online, the homeowner called TSR — who lined the same root-damaged line for $9,800 in under six hours, with no digging and no damage to the yard.
body:
The situation

A San Juan Capistrano homeowner had already gotten a quote to fix his failing sewer, and it was a shock: another plumber wanted about $18,000 to excavate and replace roughly 76 feet of sewer line running out to the main. Faced with that number, he went online to research his options and learned about cured-in-place pipe (CIPP) — a trenchless way to rebuild a sewer without digging up the yard. That is when he called TSR.

Bob from TSR came out the next day and ran a camera down the line. The pipe had not collapsed; it showed two minor offsets, and roots from a large ficus tree in the front yard had found their way in and were prying the line open. A cracked-but-intact pipe like that is a strong candidate for lining.

The fix

Instead of trenching the front yard, TSR quoted $9,800 to line the full 76-foot run — a little more than half the excavation bid — and scheduled the work just three days out. On the day of the job, the crew cleaned the roots and scale out of the pipe and cured a new resin liner in place through the existing access, sealing the two offsets and shutting the roots out for good.

The whole repair took under six hours, and it happened while the homeowner was at work. He came home to a brand-new sewer pipe and a front yard exactly as he had left it — no trench, no torn-up landscaping, and no five-figure excavation bill.

Why it worked here

Getting a second opinion paid off. Because the pipe was cracked and root-infiltrated but still held its shape, it could be relined rather than replaced — which is what turned an $18,000 dig into a same-morning, $9,800 trenchless repair. Not every line qualifies: a collapsed or badly offset pipe still needs bursting or excavation, and running the camera first is what tells the difference.

title: 81 ft of root-invaded clay sewer and drain line CIPP lined in Pasadena
summary: TSR opened one 3x3 pit in the lawn, cleared roots to the city sewer, CIPP lined 51 feet of clay with a transition liner sealed at the city connection, then lined another 30 feet of drain line from the curb.
body:
The pipe

Pasadena's residential sewers are some of the oldest still in service in Southern California, and much of that pipe is vitrified clay. Clay is strong in compression but it comes in short lengths, and every bell joint is a gap roots can exploit. On this property, roots had grown into the house sewer along its run to the public main.

Under the City of Pasadena's rules, the private house sewer starts 24 inches outside the building wall and runs all the way to the city line, which is often a manhole out in the street. That makes the full run the owner's responsibility, and it's why a cured-in-place liner that covers it end to end is worth so much here.

How the lining was done

TSR's crew excavated a single access pit in a grass area, about 3 feet square and 4 feet deep, and disconnected the line. From that pit they cut out every root from the house side to the public sewer, which a liner needs before it can seat against the host pipe.

The run was relined with 51 feet of epoxy CIPP. Because the pipe diameter changes along the way, a transition liner was specified so it changes diameter along with the host pipe instead of wrinkling or bridging at the change. The liner was pushed roughly two inches into the city sewer and trimmed flush, which seals the final joint, the connection between private lateral and public main and a spot where roots commonly get back in.

After cure, the line was reconnected with ABS and the pit backfilled and re-sodded.

A second line from the curb

A second drain line was then handled from the curb: roots cleared and 30 feet lined with the same epoxy system, for 81 feet of rehabilitated pipe on one property and no trench anywhere.

Permits for CIPP in Pasadena

Pasadena Public Works treats relining as a permitted repair. Its published guidance calls for CCTV video of the line before and after lining, submitted with the permit, along with a refundable deposit. If you're getting quotes for lining in Pasadena, ask whether the contractor handles that video submittal. A verified CIPP installer should.

Why lining fits Pasadena

Between protected street and yard trees, landmark-district hardscape and century-old laterals, excavation in Pasadena gets expensive long before the plumbing does. A clay line that still holds its shape is usually a good CIPP candidate, and a single access pit keeps restoration to a patch of lawn.

title: 70 ft sewer lateral with a pipe-size change CIPP lined to the city main in Los Angeles
summary: One 3x4 pit at the bend in the line gave TSR access to reline 70 feet to the public main with a transition liner, rebuild the fitting at the turn and add a two-way cleanout.
body:
Why this lateral mattered to the owner

In the City of Los Angeles, the property owner is responsible for the house connection lateral all the way from the property line to the connection at the main, including root problems in the public right-of-way. So a lining job that stops at the property line leaves the owner holding the most exposed part of the pipe. This project lined the full run to the city sewer.

The site conditions

Two features of this lateral usually steer contractors toward a dig: a bend midway between house and street, and a change in pipe diameter. TSR's approach was to dig once, at the turn, with a pit about 3 by 4 feet and 3 feet deep. Working at the bend gave access to both straight sections and allowed the elbow itself to be replaced.

The lining

After clearing the remaining roots toward the city connection, 70 feet of epoxy cured-in-place liner went in. A transition liner handled the size change so the liner stays tight to the host pipe on both sides of it. The liner was carried about two inches into the public sewer and cut flush, closing the last joint on the owner's line.

Access for the future

At the turn, the crew installed new ABS pipe and a two-way cleanout, then backfilled. With a two-way cleanout, a camera or jetter can be sent upstream or downstream from the same fitting, which makes future inspections simpler for the owner and for any buyer's inspector.

Permits in Los Angeles

City code requires an S-Permit to repair a house connection sewer, and work in the right-of-way needs a bonded sewer contractor with inspection by Building and Safety. When comparing CIPP bids in Los Angeles, confirm who pulls that permit and whether the price includes lining past the property line to the main.

title: 90 ft of sewer CIPP lined in Seal Beach, from under the house out to the city sewer
summary: From a single pit beside the existing cleanout, TSR lined 70 feet to the city with a 4x6 transition liner, then descaled and lined 20 feet of cast iron under the home and reopened its branch connection.
body:
Owner-maintained, end to end

Seal Beach Public Works puts maintenance of the sewer lateral on the homeowner all the way to the sewer main. Much of the city's housing went up between the 1940s and the late 1960s, so a large share of those laterals and under-slab drains are now well past half a century old.

Access from the existing cleanout

TSR dug one pit, about 3 by 3 feet and 3 feet deep, right beside the cleanout already on the property. The line was disconnected there, and remaining roots were cleared to the city connection.

Lateral: 70 feet with a 4x6 transition liner

The lateral steps between 4-inch and 6-inch diameter, so the crew installed a 4x6 transition liner, 70 feet long, ending two inches inside the city sewer and trimmed flush. Matching the liner to both diameters avoids the wrinkles and loose sections a single-size liner leaves at a size change.

Under the house: 20 feet of cast iron

Inside, the building drain was cast iron with typical internal scale. The crew descaled 20 feet of it back to sound metal and lined it with epoxy CIPP, then reinstated the one branch connection on that section by cutting it open from inside the new liner. No flooring was removed.

Finish

A two-way cleanout was installed at the pit so either direction can be inspected or cleaned later. Total: 90 feet of rehabilitated pipe, one excavation.

What to ask for in Seal Beach

Coastal cast iron and aging laterals often fail together. When you get a CIPP quote, ask whether it covers the building drain under the slab as well as the lateral to the main, and how branch connections will be reinstated.

title: 100 ft of cast iron and clay sewer CIPP lined in San Diego with five branch reinstatements
summary: Working from one pit at the cast-to-clay joint in the driveway, TSR spent about seven hours descaling 80 feet of cast iron, lined it with CIPP, reinstated five branch lines and lined 20 feet of clay downstream.
body:
Who owns the lateral in San Diego

The City of San Diego's Sewer System Management Plan is blunt about it: the city owns no part of the service lateral. The property owner is responsible for maintenance and repair from the building all the way to the wye at the sewer main. With roughly 280,000 privately owned laterals in the city, the condition of that pipe is squarely a homeowner issue.

The dig

This home had cast iron running back toward the house and clay heading to the street, joined under the driveway. TSR saw-cut the concrete and opened a pit about 3 by 4 feet and 4 feet deep at that joint and disconnected the line, giving access upstream and downstream from one spot.

Descaling before lining

Roughly 80 feet of the cast iron, running to the back of the home, was heavily scaled. The crew descaled the full length and flushed the loosened material out with high-pressure water, about seven hours of work in all. That step is what allows an epoxy liner to bond to the host pipe. Liners installed over scale tend to delaminate or wrinkle.

Lining and reinstatement

The crew then installed 80 feet of epoxy CIPP to the back of the home. Five branch lines tie into that run, and each opening was found and reopened with a cutter working inside the new pipe. Downstream, 20 feet of the clay was lined as well, so the rehabilitated section doesn't end at an old clay joint.

Finish

A dual sweep cleanout was installed at the pit, and the dirt and cement were restored. Total rehabilitated length: 100 feet.

San Diego takeaway

When a quote for cast iron lining doesn't mention descaling time or how many branch connections will be reinstated, ask. Those two items separate a durable CIPP job from a quick one.

title: 40 ft of 2-inch kitchen drain CIPP lined under a Tustin home without opening the floor
summary: TSR reached the kitchen line by tunneling two feet under the house from a 3x3 pit, descaled and hydro jetted 40 feet of 2-inch pipe (about six hours), lined it to the main and added an exterior cleanout.
body:
Small pipe, same problem

CIPP gets talked about mostly for 4-inch and 6-inch sewer laterals, but the same process works on the 2-inch drains inside a house. Kitchen lines are often first to go: grease and food waste stick to the rough interior of old pipe, and scale builds on scale until the line barely flows.

Reaching it from outside

The drain passed beneath the home on its way to the building sewer. TSR set up below the kitchen window, where the owner had removed a shrub. A 3-by-3-foot pit, 3 feet deep, went in there, and a short tunnel of about two feet under the foundation line brought the crew to the kitchen drain, where it was disconnected. Nothing inside the home was opened.

Cleaning a 2-inch line

Descaling the 2-inch pipe to the main, 40 feet in all, and jetting out the loosened scale took about six hours. Small-diameter lining depends on that cleaning even more than larger pipe does, because there's less margin for buildup under the liner.

The liner and a new cleanout

Forty feet of epoxy CIPP followed, ending as near the main as the tie-in permitted. To give the owner future access, a strip of stucco roughly 18 inches wide was removed beneath the window down to the excavation, and a cleanout plus a short new pipe section were fitted back to where the line had been cut. The wall was sealed and re-stuccoed, the concrete at the foundation patched, and the pit filled. Painting was not included.

A note on Tustin sewers

Tustin's sewer service is split between the city and Irvine Ranch Water District depending on location. In IRWD's area, the district maintains the lower lateral from its collection system to the easement or right-of-way line, and the owner maintains the upper lateral and everything inside, which includes a kitchen line like this one.

title: Offset joints ground out and 75 ft of sewer CIPP lined to the city in Tarzana
summary: The Tarzana lateral had offsets and cracks that would have blocked a liner. TSR ground them smooth from inside, then installed 75 feet of epoxy transition liner trimmed flush at the city connection.
body:
Offsets: the usual reason lining gets ruled out

An offset is a misaligned joint: two lengths of pipe that no longer line up. Small ones catch paper and invite roots. Larger ones leave a ledge a liner can't pass cleanly, and a liner cured over a ledge ends up with a hump or a wrinkle. Many contractors see offsets on camera and quote a dig.

The Tarzana lateral on this job had several of them, plus cracking, along its run toward the public main.

Grinding first

TSR excavated one pit, about 3 by 3 feet and 4 feet deep in dirt, and disconnected the line. A grinder run through the pipe knocked down each misaligned joint and rough crack out to the public sewer, opening a path the liner could travel and cure against.

Lining with a transition liner

The pipe also changes size along the run, so a 75-foot epoxy transition liner was used. It extends into the public connection and was cut flush there, sealing the joint where the private lateral meets the public main.

Finish

The line was reconnected in the pit with ABS pipe and the dirt backfilled.

Tarzana permits

Tarzana sits inside Los Angeles city limits, so the same rules apply as anywhere in the city: the owner is responsible for the lateral to the main, and repairs to the house connection sewer require an S-Permit. Valley lots with shifting soil tend to develop offsets over time, so a camera inspection that measures how far joints have moved is the first step before deciding between grinding and lining, a point repair, or replacement.

title: 50 ft of cracked, root-filled cast iron CIPP lined in Ojai with robotic reinstatement
summary: From a pit beside the existing cleanout, TSR spent about six hours descaling 50 feet of cracked cast iron with roots, lined it up to the plastic pipe and reopened two branch lines with a robotic cutter.
body:
Cracks plus roots

Cast iron usually fails from the inside out as rust and scale thin the wall. Once it cracks, roots follow, and the roots widen the cracks as they grow. That's where this Ojai line was when TSR got the call.

Access

TSR dug one pit in dirt, about 3 feet square and 3 feet deep, next to the existing cleanout, and disconnected the cleanout to open the line. Starting from a cleanout keeps the excavation small and puts the crew right on the pipe.

Descaling

The crew descaled 50 feet of the cast iron, cutting out roots and grinding away scale, which took about six hours, and water-jetted the line clean. Epoxy bonds only to clean metal, so this stage sets the life of the liner.

Lining to the transition

Fifty feet of epoxy CIPP was installed, ending at the joint with the downstream plastic pipe. The plastic section was sound, so the liner ended where the failing iron ended.

Robotic reinstatement

Two branch lines tie into that section. After cure, the crew sent a robotic cutter inside the new liner to locate and reopen both connections from within, with no digging at either branch. The cleanout was then reconnected and the pit backfilled.

CIPP in the Ojai Valley

Ojai is served by TSR out of its Southern California coverage that includes all of Ventura County. For older cast iron with cracks and roots, ask any lining contractor how they'll descale, how long they've budgeted for it, and how branch connections will be reopened. Robotic reinstatement from inside the pipe is the standard to look for.

title: 172 ft of sewer CIPP lined in three directions from a single pit in Palm Springs
summary: TSR dug one pit at the wye and lined three runs: 90 feet to the city with the neighbor's line reinstated, 34 feet toward the kitchen with 10 feet of epoxy coating through a tight bend, and 48 feet with a transition liner.
body:
A branching system

This Palm Springs property's sewer split at a wye into three runs: one out to the public sewer, one back toward the kitchen and rear bath, and one running along the opposite side of the home. Replacing that by trenching would have meant three trenches through desert landscaping. TSR did it from one excavation.

Scope: 172 feet of epoxy CIPP lining and 10 feet of epoxy coating.

The pit

A pit about 3 by 4 feet and 4 feet deep was dug at the wye, exposing the junction where all three runs meet.

Run 1: 90 feet to the city

Roots were cleared to the city connection and 90 feet of liner installed, ending two inches inside the public sewer and trimmed flush. This run also carries flow from the house next door, and that tie-in was reopened from within the liner once it cured.

Run 2: toward the kitchen and back bath

This leg got 44 feet of descaling, then jetting, then 34 feet of liner as far as a hard 90-degree elbow. Rather than force a liner around it, the crew pulled the toilet and applied epoxy coating over the last 10 feet from the fixture side, lapping onto the end of the liner so the two seal together. The kitchen line and cleanout were reinstated.

Run 3: 48 feet with a transition liner

The third run was descaled for 48 feet, stopping at plastic pipe, and relined for all 48 feet using a transition liner because the diameter changes along that leg. The line was reconnected in ABS and the pit backfilled with the dirt and rock.

Why this job is a good model

Multi-branch systems are where CIPP saves the most. The keys are an access point at the junction, reinstatement of every tie-in (including a neighbor's), and the right tool for each segment: full liners for long straight runs, transition liners for size changes, and coating for elbows a liner can't negotiate.

title: 64 ft of coastal cast iron CIPP lined and a toilet branch epoxy coated in Hermosa Beach
summary: From one pit in a flower bed, TSR descaled and lined 60 feet of cast iron to the clay transition plus 4 feet under the home, then descaled and epoxy coated the toilet branch line.
body:
The coastal cast iron problem

South Bay beach towns combine two things that are hard on sewers: cast iron drain pipe, which corrodes faster in salt air and near-surface groundwater, and small lots mostly covered by house and hardscape. Trenching is rarely even possible, so lining is usually the only practical repair.

One pit in a flower bed

The only unpaved spot above the line was a planting bed at the entry, and that's where TSR dug its 3-by-3-foot, 3-foot-deep pit. It gave access both toward the street and back beneath the house.

Descaling

Descaling covered 60 feet of the downstream cast iron, up to the change to clay, and another 10 feet beneath the house. Jetting removed the loosened scale.

Lining

Liner went into the full 60-foot downstream run and 4 feet of the pipe beneath the house, sealing corrosion and cracks inside a new continuous pipe.

Epoxy coating the toilet branch

Branch lines are small and bend tightly, which suits epoxy coating better than a liner. The toilet was pulled, the branch descaled out to the main line, epoxy coated, and the toilet reset.

Finish

After the connection in the pit was remade, the planting bed was filled back in.

For South Bay homeowners

If you're in Hermosa Beach, Manhattan Beach or Redondo Beach with original cast iron, a camera inspection will show where the cast iron ends and clay begins, and whether branch lines need coating as well as the main run lining.
